rationale: A wins because it has the one thing founders usually lack: restraint. Its refusal that the lawsuit is “a question every reporter will ask, not an angle the company can own” is grown-up PR judgment; B leads with “arrives with the company mid-lawsuit over corporate espionage,” which turns legal baggage into the pitch without proving the lawsuit connects to the product. A’s strongest angle, “It won't say how often it's wrong,” names the real story and the missing proof cleanly.
gaps_in_A: “Deel is now automating that call” pushes a little past the facts; the update says the tool flags risks, not that it makes legal determinations.

“A $12B payroll company just made AI compliance a free feature, not a product” is useful but slightly over-clean; “included for existing customers” does not prove permanence, new-customer pricing, or no hidden packaging change.
“One employer, one bad contractor call” only works with a named customer and real flag; A says that, but the headline still reads more concrete than the evidence supplied.
gaps_in_B: “Deel's new AI compliance tool arrives with the company mid-lawsuit over corporate espionage” is the wrong lead angle for Deel to pitch unless the lawsuit directly touches this product; B never proves that connection.
“a deliberate reputational move” invents motive. That is courtroom-adjacent speculation, not an angle you hand to a reporter unless you enjoy stepping on rakes.
“budget question for HR teams' outside counsel” assumes customers currently use outside counsel for this exact work and might replace it; the update does not supply spend, behavior, or a named buyer.
“business or legal-affairs reporter” is still too broad for the lawsuit angle; the set gestures at a beat instead of pinning the actual coverage lane.
